title: Beta-Caryophyllene: The Peppery Terpene Explained
h1: What Is the Caryophyllene Terpene? The Peppery Compound Linked to CB2
metaDescription: Beta-caryophyllene, the peppery terpene in black pepper, cloves and cannabis: its CB2 link, what research shows so far and how to look for it in lab results.
excerpt: Beta-caryophyllene is a major part of black pepper's essential oil and shows up in many cannabis strains. Here's what makes it unusual, what research has and hasn't shown, and where to look for it in lab results.
keyTakeaways: Beta-caryophyllene is a spicy, woody terpene found in black pepper, cloves, hops and many cannabis strains.
A 2008 lab study found it binds to and activates the CB2 receptor, though a 2019 study did not detect that activity.
It doesn't act on CB1, the receptor behind THC's high, so it isn't intoxicating on its own.
Findings on inflammation, microbes, mood and cancer come mostly from cell and animal studies, not human trials.
Strain names are unreliable guides to terpenes; a batch's lab report is the better check.
body:
The caryophyllene terpene, beta-caryophyllene, is one of the main compounds in black pepper's essential oil, and cannabis plants make plenty of it too. It stands out for one reason: a 2008 study found that it binds to CB2, one of the body's cannabinoid receptors, which earned it the nickname “dietary cannabinoid.” Here's what it is, where it's found, what research has and hasn't shown, and where it turns up in lab results.

## Terpenes in brief

Terpenes are the aromatic compounds behind a plant's scent, and cannabis produces them in the resin glands that also make its cannabinoids. They're why one strain smells like citrus and another like pine or pepper.

A 2022 analysis of lab results from six U.S. states, including Michigan, had terpene data for about 43,000 flower samples. Myrcene, beta-caryophyllene and limonene came out on top, with the highest average levels. Individual terpenes rarely made up more than 0.5% of a sample's weight. Our [terpene guide](/blog/what-are-cannabis-terpenes/) introduces the rest of the family.

## What the caryophyllene terpene is

Beta-caryophyllene is a sesquiterpene, a larger, less volatile molecule than light terpenes such as limonene. You'll see it written as BCP or (E)-beta-caryophyllene. It's common in the essential oils of spices, fruits and other plants.

It's also a familiar food ingredient: U.S. and European regulators allow beta-caryophyllene as a food additive and flavoring, so it's already part of many diets. When it oxidizes, it can form caryophyllene oxide, a related compound that behaves differently in the body.

## Caryophyllene and CB2: what makes it unusual

Your body has two main cannabinoid receptors. CB1 is concentrated in the brain and drives THC's high, while CB2 is found mainly on immune cells. Our [endocannabinoid system explainer](/blog/what-is-the-endocannabinoid-system/) covers how they work.

In 2008, researchers reported that beta-caryophyllene binds selectively to CB2 and activates it, while leaving CB1 alone. In mice, an oral dose reduced an induced inflammatory response, but not in mice bred without CB2 receptors.

The story isn't settled. In a 2019 lab study, beta-caryophyllene and five other terpenes common in cannabis failed to activate CB1 or CB2, nor did they alter THC's activity at those receptors. That study measured one signaling pathway, so effects through other pathways remain possible. For now, the CB2 link is an intriguing lab finding, not proof of an effect in people.

## Aroma and taste: black pepper, clove and wood

Beta-caryophyllene smells spicy and woody, like freshly cracked black pepper with a hint of clove. In cannabis, it adds a peppery, earthy edge. It often travels with humulene: in the 2022 lab-data study, the two rose and fell together, a sign that the same plant enzymes help make both. Our [humulene guide](/blog/humulene-the-earthy-terpene/) covers its earthy partner.

## Where it's found: pepper, cloves, hops and cannabis

- **Black pepper**, where it's a major part of the essential oil (the bite comes from a different compound, piperine).
- **Cloves**, whose oil is rich in it.
- **Hops**, alongside humulene, which is named after the hop plant.
- **Herbs** such as rosemary and basil.
- **Cannabis**, where it's among the most abundant terpenes.

That list is a reminder that the peppery terpene is part of everyday food, not just cannabis.

## Caryophyllene effects: what research is exploring

Most claims about caryophyllene benefits trace back to cells and animals, so hold these findings loosely:

- **Inflammation.** Lab and animal studies, including the 2008 mouse work, suggest it can dial down inflammatory signals. Reviews list anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity among its experimental effects.
- **Microbes.** Experimental studies have reported antimicrobial activity in lab tests.
- **Mood.** In a 2014 study, mice given beta-caryophyllene behaved in ways researchers associate with less anxiety and depression, and the effects disappeared when CB2 was blocked.

Mouse behavior and lab dishes don't reliably predict what happens in people. Nothing here shows that beta-caryophyllene, or a strain rich in it, will ease inflammation, infection, anxiety or low mood. If you're managing any of those, talk with your clinician.

## Cancer research: early lab findings only

You may see caryophyllene mentioned in cancer research. A 2016 review found that it and caryophyllene oxide slowed the growth of various cancer cells in lab studies. The review also noted that these effects had hardly been tested in living animals, let alone people. That's preclinical research: it helps scientists choose what to study next, and it's no basis for using a terpene, or cannabis, to manage cancer. Anyone facing cancer should rely on their oncology team.

## Strains high in caryophyllene, and checking lab reports

Strain names are shaky guides to chemistry, but some show patterns. In the 2022 analysis, samples fell into a few chemical groups, and one was defined by high caryophyllene and limonene. Products sold as Purple Punch landed in that group 96% of the time. Other names were far less consistent: only about 62% of products sold as Tangie fell into any single group.

Use a strain name as a hint and the lab report as the answer:

- Look for a terpene panel in the batch's lab results, when one is available.
- Compare beta-caryophyllene with myrcene and limonene to see which leads.
- Expect small numbers: most individual terpenes measure well under 1% of the flower.

For how terpenes and cannabinoids might work together, see [the entourage effect](/blog/the-entourage-effect/). Our guide to [cannabis terpene blends](/blog/cannabis-terpene-blends/) covers products with added terpenes. Curious about a product's terpene profile? Stop by one of our [Michigan stores](/dispensary-locations/) and ask a budtender. Recreational shopping starts at age 21. Use cannabis responsibly.

faq.a: Spicy and woody, like freshly cracked black pepper with a hint of clove. In cannabis, it adds a peppery, earthy edge, and it often shows up alongside humulene, a woody terpene shared with hops. How strongly you notice it depends on the strain's full terpene mix and how fresh the flower is.

Not in the usual sense. It's a terpene, a different chemical family from THC, CBD and the other cannabinoids. Researchers nicknamed it a dietary cannabinoid after a 2008 study found it binds to the CB2 receptor. A 2019 study didn't detect that activity, so the nickname is still debated.

No. THC produces its high by activating CB1 receptors in the brain, and beta-caryophyllene doesn't act on CB1. It's also a common food flavoring found in black pepper and cloves, and eating those doesn't make anyone high. In cannabis, it shapes aroma and flavor, while THC is what produces intoxication.

faq.q: Which strains have the most caryophyllene?
faq.a: It varies from batch to batch. In a large 2022 study of U.S. lab data, products sold as Purple Punch fell into a high-caryophyllene, high-limonene group 96% of the time. Many other strain names were inconsistent. The surest way to know is the terpene panel on the lab report for the batch in front of you.

claims.claim: Beta-caryophyllene 'gives black pepper its warm bite' (opening) / 'gives black pepper its bite' (excerpt).
claims.fix: Black pepper's bite (pungency) comes from the alkaloid piperine; beta-caryophyllene is a leading compound of black pepper's essential oil (9.4-30.9% of fruit oil). Reworded in the body and the excerpt.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17987447/ (Srinivasan 2007 abstract: black pepper 'is valued for its distinct biting quality attributed to the alkaloid, piperine'); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6479398/ (Salehi 2019 Piper review, Europe PMC full text: Table 11, beta-caryophyllene 9.4-30.9% of P. nigrum fruit essential oil; 'its pungent principle component, piperine')

claims.claim: Black pepper, 'where it carries much of the spicy aroma'.
claims.fix: No source opened says beta-caryophyllene carries black pepper's aroma; it is a major oil component. Reworded to 'a major part of the essential oil (the bite comes from a different compound, piperine)'.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6479398/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17987447/

claims.claim: A 2008 study found beta-caryophyllene binds CB2, earning the nickname 'dietary cannabinoid'.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2449371/ (Gertsch 2008, 'Beta-caryophyllene is a dietary cannabinoid', abstract via Europe PMC)

claims.claim: Cannabis makes terpenes in the same resin glands that make its cannabinoids.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ (glandular trichomes produce cannabinoids and terpenes; opened for the trichome article in this batch)

claims.claim: A 2022 analysis of nearly 90,000 lab samples from six U.S. states, including Michigan: myrcene, beta-caryophyllene and limonene highest on average; individual terpenes rarely above 0.5% of weight.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9119530/ (Smith 2022, Europe PMC full text: n = 89,923; six US states incl. PSI Labs, Michigan; 'myrcene, beta-caryophyllene, and limonene were present at the highest levels'; 'rarely present at more than 0.5% weight')

claims.claim: Beta-caryophyllene is a sesquiterpene, larger and less volatile than monoterpenes such as limonene; written BCP or (E)-beta-caryophyllene.
claims.source: general chemistry (C15 sesquiterpene vs C10 monoterpene); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2449371/ ('(E)-beta-caryophyllene [(E)-BCP]')

claims.claim: It's common in the essential oils of spices, fruits and other plants.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2449371/ ('a common constituent of the essential oils of numerous spice and food plants')

claims.claim: U.S. and European regulators allow beta-caryophyllene as a food additive and flavoring.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26965491/ (Sharma 2016 abstract: 'approved by United States Food and Drug Administration and European agencies as food additive, taste enhancer and flavoring agent')

claims.claim: Oxidized, it can form caryophyllene oxide, which behaves differently (no CB1/CB2 binding).
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5083753/ (Fidyt 2016: BCP converted to caryophyllene-5,6-oxide; 'BCPO, does not exhibit CB1/2 binding')

claims.claim: CB1 is concentrated in the brain and drives THC's high; CB2 is found mainly on immune cells.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2449371/ ('the CB(1) receptor is responsible for the psychomodulatory effects'); CB2 distribution is general pharmacology

claims.claim: 2008: beta-caryophyllene binds selectively to CB2 and activates it, not CB1; oral dose reduced induced inflammation in mice but not in CB2-knockout mice.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2449371/ ('selectively binds to the CB(2) receptor ... functional CB(2) agonist'; 'peroral (E)-BCP at 5 mg/kg strongly reduces the carrageenan-induced inflammatory response in wild-type mice but not in mice lacking CB(2) receptors'); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5083753/ ('strong affinity to CB2, but not CB1')

claims.claim: 2019 lab study: beta-caryophyllene and five other common terpenes did not activate CB1 or CB2 or alter THC's activity; one signaling pathway measured, so others remain possible.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6757242/ (Santiago 2019, Europe PMC full text: 'The terpenoids tested did not activate CB1 or CB2 by themselves, nor did they modify the signaling of ... delta-9-THC'; 'It remains possible that terpenoids activate CB1 and CB2 signaling pathways that do not involve potassium channels')

claims.claim: It smells spicy and woody, like black pepper with a hint of clove.
claims.source: sensory description; no factual claim beyond aroma

claims.claim: It often travels with humulene; in the 2022 study the two correlated, as terpenes co-produced by common enzymes.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9119530/ ('correlation between beta-caryophyllene and humulene, two Cannabis terpenes co-produced by common enzymes')

claims.claim: Found in cloves (whose oil is rich in it), hops, rosemary and basil, and among the most abundant terpenes in cannabis.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5083753/ (BCP 'commonly found in basil, cinnamon, black pepper, cloves, cannabis, lavender, oregano, and rosemary'); clove essential oil review PMC8588428 abstract via Europe PMC ('rich in volatile compounds and antioxidants such as eugenol, beta-caryophyllene, and alpha-humulene'); hops and humulene's name (Humulus) are general knowledge; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9119530/ (cannabis)

claims.claim: Inflammation: lab and animal studies suggest it can reduce inflammatory signals; reviews list anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity as experimental effects.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26965491/ ('antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and immune-modulator have been reported in experimental studies'); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2449371/

claims.claim: Microbes: experimental studies report antimicrobial activity in lab tests.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26965491/

claims.claim: 2014 mouse study: beta-caryophyllene produced anxiety- and depression-related behavioral changes that disappeared when CB2 was blocked.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24930711/ (Bahi 2014 abstract: 'pre-administration of the CB2 receptor antagonist AM630, fully abrogated the anxiolytic and the anti-depressant effects of BCP')

claims.claim: Nothing shows that beta-caryophyllene or a strain rich in it eases inflammation, infection, anxiety or low mood; talk with a clinician.
claims.source: consistent with the preclinical-only evidence above; Michigan R 420.507 (facts/law-facts.json mi-advertising)

claims.claim: A 2016 review: BCP and caryophyllene oxide slowed growth of various cancer cells in the lab, but had hardly been tested in living animals.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5083753/ ('significant anticancer activities, affecting growth and proliferation of numerous cancer cells. Nevertheless, their antineoplastic effects have hardly been investigated in vivo.')

claims.claim: In the 2022 analysis, one chemical group was high caryophyllene-limonene; Purple Punch products landed there 96% of the time; only 62.5% of Tangie products fell into one group.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9119530/ ('96% of product averages attached to Purple Punch fall within Cluster I (high caryophyllene-limonene), while only 62.5% of product averages for Tangie fall into a single cluster')

claims.claim: Most individual terpenes measure well under 1% of the flower.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9119530/ ('rarely present at more than 0.5% weight and most were present at low levels (< 0.2%)')

claims.claim: It doesn't act on CB1 and isn't intoxicating on its own; eating pepper or cloves doesn't make anyone high.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2449371/ ('functional nonpsychoactive CB(2) receptor ligand in foodstuff')

review.notes: Independent fact-check 2026-10-24 (batch 9). Opened: Santiago 2019, Fidyt 2016 and Smith 2022 (Europe PMC full text); Gertsch 2008, Sharma 2016 and Bahi 2014 (Europe PMC abstract records); for the fix, Srinivasan 2007 (abstract) and the Salehi 2019 Piper review (full text). The six listed sources exist, are https and support their sentences; the two pepper sources are recorded here only, to keep the list at six. Two claims fixed (three text edits): beta-caryophyllene does not give black pepper its bite (piperine does; body and excerpt), and 'carries much of the spicy aroma' was unsupported. Cross-batch sweep 2026-10-24 (orchestrator, after the fact-check workflow): Smith et al. 2022 (PLoS One, PMC9119530, full text re-read through NCBI efetch) analyzed 89,923 samples, but only 42,843 had terpene data; its terpene, chemotype and label findings rest on that subset (the label comparison is "in terms of terpene profile"), so the sample count in this article now names the subset.
review.writerNotes: Medical article: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links; the in-store pointer goes to /dispensary-locations/ only. Re-read and revised 2026-10-24: the opening line and one FAQ answer rewritten to remove phrasing shared with other published pages, the budtender line no longer implies High Society hands out lab reports (not published), and the herb list trimmed to rosemary and basil (general knowledge). The H1 says "linked to CB2" rather than "acts on CB2" because the 2019 study did not reproduce CB2 activation. Black pepper, clove and hops as sources are general knowledge. Strain names are cultivar names, not brands.
